episodes.206233: Abnormally high moisture amounts and considerable instability, along with a weak disturbance, induced a couple of rounds of thunderstorms.
episodes.206244: An upper level approaching shortwave ushered a cold front at the surface with an outflow boundary into Arkansas which led to multiple severe thunderstorms with large hail and damaging winds.
episodes.206302: Typical summertime pulse thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening hours of September 14-17. While most storms remained below severe limits, a few storms did produce localized damaging downburst winds and large hail.
episodes.206366: An upper level trough with an embedded shortwave aloft produced isolated showers and thunderstorms in Southwest MT late afternoon through the evening. Weak shear kept most thunderstorms sub-severe. However, there was enough instability and moisture for a few storms to become severe and produce gusty winds.
episodes.206808: Isolated strong to severe thunderstorms developed across far eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon and early evening of the 15th. Moderate instability developed during the afternoon in the hot and humid air mass, but wind fields and wind shear were very weak. This combination of instability and wind shear resulted in intense, but short-lived thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced hail up to penny size and damaging downburst wind gusts.
episodes.207001: A stationary front was located on the northern edge of the Quad State throughout the day on the 14th. A localized low pressure area over the Quad State helped generate scattered showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours on the 14th. These storms generally tracked southwestward through Southern Illinois, Southeast Missouri, and far Western Kentucky.  MLCAPE values were 1000-2000J/kg with DCAPE at 1200-1400J/kg in Southern Illinois. Effective bulk shear was limited to under 30kts. While a couple areas had quarter size hail spotted, straight-line wind damage was the primary severe weather hazard. Particularly robust downburst winds were observed in Franklin and Jackson Counties in Southern Illinois with heavy tree damage to a campground off of Rend Lake and a line of damage from a storm tracking southwestward in Jackson County. A downburst in Saline County overturned and partially destroyed an anchored single-wide trailer.
episodes.207002: A stationary front was located on the northern edge of the Quad State throughout the day on the 14th. A localized low pressure area over the Quad State helped generate scattered showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours on the 14th. MLCAPE values were 1000-2000J/kg with DCAPE at 1000-1300J/kg in far Western Kentucky. Effective bulk shear was limited to under 30kts. Damage reports in Western Kentucky were limited to a large tree limb and blown over basketball goal with a storm moving through Fulton County.
episodes.207003: Enhanced moisture convergence near a surface low allowed a few storms to develop over the Ozark Foothills of southeast Missouri in the afternoon. With high pressure aloft centered north of the area, wind shear was very weak, but surface-based CAPE was around 2000 J/kg. As they moved southward in the late afternoon, one storm produced some hail near the Arkansas border south of Gatewood.
episodes.207096: Scattered thunderstorms developed in Missouri along a backdoor cold front during the afternoon of September 15th. An unstable but weakly sheared environment with steep low-level lapse rates resulted in the potential for microbursts from these thunderstorms. A few microbursts did occur, with wind damage ranging from downed trees to a partially removed school roof.
episodes.207263: A strong low pressure system moved out of the North Pacific Ocean on September 14th and into the Gulf of Alaska through September 15th. The weather front associated with this strong low tapped into sub-tropical moisture as it lifted out of the North Pacific and transported this moisture in a very narrow but long plume which is described as an atmospheric river. ||This atmospheric river moved over the Ketchikan area of Southeast Alaska through Monday and produced very heavy, localized, rain for approximately 12 hours. Area precipitation stations reported a range of rainfall amounts of 2 to 8 inches throughout the duration of the event (36hrs), including a new daily rainfall record for the airport and the 4th wettest day on record ever. When looking at rainfall intensity return periods, this 24 hour amount was a 5 year return period, but most of that fell in a 12 hour period with 6.60 inches from 0700AKST to 1900AKST (a 25 year return period). Looking at a finer scale, the 6 hour amount at the Ketchikan airport of 3.94 inches was a 10 year return period. ||This very heavy and record breaking rainfall produced significant runoff across the Ketchikan area. This significant runoff produced mainly urban flooding of roads causing road closures and did raise area hydroelectric dams significantly.
episodes.207425: A mid-level trough axis tracked across western Kansas. Mesoanalysis a few hours prior should rapidly developing instability below a cool mid-level. Flow and shear were also sufficient for severe storm development. In the late afternoon/evening, a line of storms developed and moved along the northern border of the CWA. A few isolated supercells developed along the southern flank of the line. The strongest of these supercells in the CWA produced a pair of 1 inch hail reports in Trego county.
episodes.207521: A low-pressure center moved north from South Dakota to North Dakota with a warm front lifting to the north. This resulted in strong low-level wind shear over central North Dakota. This shear combined with low cloud bases caused by a high amount of moisture in the lower atmosphere to produce multiple low-topped supercells which produced a low amount of lighting. From these supercells, 20 tornadoes developed over central North Dakota which moved in a generally southerly to northerly direction. Two tornadoes produced EF-2 damage. Near Denhoff in Sheridan County, multiple buildings including mobile homes and farm out-buildings were severely damaged along the tornado path, along with damage to many trees and some vehicles. This multi-vortex tornado had a total path length of approximately 13 miles. The second area of EF-2 tornado damage was about 13 miles west of Linton in Emmons County, where a barn was destroyed near Beaver Bay. Two other tornadoes produced EF-1 damage. Near Menoken in Burleigh County, there was damage to trees and the roof of a farm outbuilding. Near Mercer in McLean County, a pole barn was partially destroyed, and a mobile home on wheels was destroyed. Numerous other tornadoes occurred with no damage to evaluate. By National Weather Service policy, those tornadoes were rated EF-U (Unknown). Otherwise, no damaging straight-line winds were reported, and the only large hail reported was one inch in diameter, which occurred near Balfour in McHenry County. In addition, flash flooding occurred over parts of Burleigh and Morton Counties as a result of the heavy rain from the storms. Many vehicles were stranded in Bismarck as multiple roads were underwater, and in Morton County several rural roads had water flowing over.
episodes.207522: Funnel clouds developed in Ward County near Minot in the afternoon hours as a low pressure system moved through northern North Dakota. Later in the evening thunderstorms moved into southwest North Dakota ahead of a short-wave trough ejecting ahead of an upper level low pressure system over southern Montana. One storm became severe producing 60 mph wind gusts northeast of Bucyrus in Adams County.
episodes.207527: A weak upper-level disturbance moving through the region helped to trigger isolated thunderstorms over northwest Tennessee during the evening hours of September 14, 2025. Sufficient wind shear and instability resulted in an isolated severe storm over Henry County that produced damaging winds.
episodes.207528: Scattered thunderstorms developed across north Mississippi during the early morning hours of September 15, 2025. Weak shear and marginal instability limited the strength of the storms. One strong storm caused some minor damage in Panola County.
episodes.207530: An upper-level disturbance moving through weak northwest flow over the Mid-South kicked off isolated showers and thunderstorms across north Mississippi during the evening hours of September 15, 2025. Enough instability was present to help a couple of storms intensify to severe limits and produce damaging winds.
episodes.207551: An outflow boundary from earlier showers and thunderstorms over the eastern Straits of Florida produced isolated gale-force wind gusts at Duck Key.
episodes.207552: A convective cloud line developed off the north side of the Lower Florida Keys.  An isolated waterspout was observed north of Boca Chica Key.
episodes.207594: Heavy shower and thunderstorm activity was observed each afternoon along the interior and western Puerto Rico. These rains saturated soils, causing a few landslides by the middle of the month.
episodes.207802: Winds around 60mph with thunderstorm complex moving from the south to the north.
episodes.208325: Iowa remained under the influence of a robust thermal ridge across the area, resulting in an unstable environment of 2000-3000 J/kg of MLCAPE but weak shear under 20 kts. There was no focused forcing mechanism in place, however by late afternoon temperatures had warm enough for diurnal thunderstorm development. Despite the lack of shear, one storm did result in half dollar sized hail in Black Hawk County.
episodes.208344: A few storms developed over Eastern Wyoming and produced some severe weather in terms of strong damaging wind gusts mainly in Weston county.

A social media post showed a landslide along PR-123 at km 28.5 in Adjuntas that sent rocks and debris onto the road, causing a partial closure. The event was attributed to heavy showers in recent days in the mountainous region.
Emergency managers reported through social media a landslide on PR-106, km 8.8 in Mayaguez, route to Las Marias and Maricao. Road closed while DTOP technical team evaluated the situation.

Through the late morning hours of September 15th reports from the local emergency manager reported significant runoff from the steep hillside that surrounds the Ketchikan area from the very heavy rain. This overland flow continued and increased into the afternoon, which flooded numerous roads that had to be closed due to the depth of water and the risk to life and property to the drivers. Some of this urban flooding did occur in poor drainage areas, during the tourist season, and affected traffic and the safety of the visitors. In the afternoon, the emergency manager reported brown water in the runoff, causing elevated concern for landslides, although no landslides were recorded from this event. The peak wind measured at the airport during this event was 44 mph at noon AKDT.||The Ketchikan airport recorded a new daily rainfall record for September 15th of 7.66 inches. This broke the previous daily record of 2.65 inches set in 1981. ||From the record rainfall, local hydro-electric dams rose significantly, ranging from 3 to 4 feet. Along Ketchikan Creek, which is fed from overflow of Ketchikan Lakes Dam, the water level rose almost 3 feet in 6 hours, cresting just below 62 feet. Even though it remained below minor flood stage of 63.5 feet, there was a lot of water moving down the creek and right through downtown Ketchikan which caused some concerns.
Nickel-sized hail fell in the town of De Witt.
